title: The Salt Seller and the Cotton Trader (ES)
summary: Two merchants cross a flooded river with salt and cotton. Birbal illustrates the poetic justice of natural elements. [ES]
full_text:
In the marketplace of Mathura, two rival merchants—Seth Hariram the salt dealer and Seth Mohanlal the cotton dealer—set out together with their pack bullocks to cross a swollen river during the monsoon.

Hariram, an arrogant and malicious man, secretly laughed at the cotton dealer: 'Look at your fluffy sacks of cotton! If a single splash of water touches them, they will absorb water, double in weight, and break your bullocks' backs!'

As they waded into the deep, turbulent current, both bullocks stumbled and fell into the swirling river water, submerging their loads for several minutes.

When they dragged the animals out onto the opposite bank:

Hariram's sacks of salt had completely dissolved into the river! His heavy sacks were empty; his entire fortune had washed away into the current!

Meanwhile, Mohanlal's cotton sacks had indeed become soaked and heavy. But when spread out beneath the hot sun on the riverbank, the cotton dried completely within three hours, undamaged and ready for sale!

Hariram wept bitterly, shaking his fist at the river.

Birbal, who was traveling past on an imperial inspection tour, observed the two merchants.

Birbal said to the weeping salt merchant:

'Hariram, you rejoiced at the thought of your neighbor's cotton becoming waterlogged and ruined.

'Yet nature has balanced the scales with poetic justice. Salt is rigid and dissolves when it meets the water it mocks; cotton is humble and flexible, yielding to moisture but drying under the sun.

'He who schemes for his brother's downfall invariably falls into the pit he wished upon another. Rejoice that your life was spared, and learn to trade with goodwill toward your fellows.'

Humbled by the lesson, the salt merchant apologized to his neighbor and resolved to abandon spite.
